Identifying High-impact Land Swap Opportunities at Pawnee National Grassland

Kayleigh Ward, Max Warnock, and Nate Hofford | Earth Data Analytics Certificate Program

This analysis identifies and ranks parcel exchanges that would reduce land fragmentation and increase contiguous federal land at Pawnee National Grassland, Weld County, Colorado.

Photo credit: U.S. Forest Service

Introduction¶

Improving ecosystem connectivity on a fragmented landscape¶

For more than 150 years, the great plains of North America have been heavily fragmented by agriculture, ranching, development, and energy production. As a result, efforts to preserve prairie ecosystems are often hindered by this "checkerboard" of different land ownership types. A prime example of this can be found at the Pawnee National Grassland in northeastern Colorado. This grassland is comprised of a checkerboard of federal land managed by the U.S. Forest Service, as well as state and private land.

Fragmented ownership limits the Forest Service's ability to manage the grassland as a unified ecosystem. Control of invasive species, grazing allotments, and wildlife habitat management are more difficult to coordinate when federal parcels are isolated from one another by intervening private or state land. A land swap can help solve this issue by consolidating disparate federal land. Land swaps are voluntary exchanges in which the Forest Service acquires a non-federal parcel and releases a federal parcel of comparable size and value.

This project, conducted in partnership with the non-profit Grasslands Unlimited, develops a geospatial workflow to identify and rank land swap opportunities that would reduce fragmentation and increase the contiguous federal land area at Pawnee National Grassland.

Figure 2. Federal contiguity patches and state parcels within the Pawnee National Grassland study boundary (Weld County, CO). Each colored region is a contiguous group of federal parcels; color indicates the group's contiguity score, with darker red indicating a higher score (more internally connected). Key Findings¶

The analysis identified 594 valid land swap proposals across the Pawnee National Grassland study area. The grassland currently contains 166 separate contiguous federal land patches, ranging from single-parcel isolates to the largest patch of approximately 58,397 acres. The top-ranked proposal by contiguity gain would merge two federal patches and add approximately 58,720 acres to a single federal block by exchanging two similarly-sized parcels (one private acquisition of 322 acres for one federal release of 290 acres, matched within the 10% area tolerance).

Of the 594 proposals, 37 involve acquire-candidate parcels that intersect active or permitted oil and gas infrastructure. These proposals are flagged in the dataset so that they can possibly be excluded from further consideration by land managers. No federal release-candidate parcels in the top proposals contain active oil and gas wells.

The full ranked proposal list, including parcel IDs, acreages, contiguity gain scores, and oil and gas flags, is available in the interactive explorer linked in the Additional Resources section below.

Why Land Fragmentation Matters¶

Landscape fragmentation is a recongized threat to biodiversity and ecosystem function across the world (Haddad et al., 2015). Fragmentation can reduce biodiversity, alter nutrient cycling, imhibit wildlife movement, and change plant successional patterns (Haddad et al., 2015; Anderson et al., 2023). At Pawnee National Grassland, fragmentation affects multiple ecologically important species and land management processes.

Black-tailed prairie dogs are considered a keystone species in shortgrass prairie systems. Their colonies support more than 150 other species, including burrowing owls, ferruginous hawks, and black-footed ferrets (Kotliar et al., 2006). Prairie dog colonies function best when they can expand and recolonize across connected patches, and isolated federal parcels surrounded by private land limit can that capacity. Similarly, pronghorn antelope require large, connected movement corridors across the grassland landscape (Millspaugh et al., 2021).

From a management perspective, contiguous federal blocks simplify the coordination of invasive species management (which can involve herbicide application), grazing rotations, and wildlife habitat management. Powers et al. (2022) demonstrated that reconnecting stranded public lands (isolated federal parcels surrounded by private ownership) produced a win-win scenario for both conservation management on federal land and private land contiguity. Targeted land swaps are one mechanism to achieve that reconnection without requiring net new federal land purchases.

Figure 3. Left: illustration of parcel contiguity. Parcels sharing a full edge are counted as part of the same contiguous patch; parcels that only touch at a corner are not. Right: the interior edge ratio used to score each federal patch. The ratio is calculated as the number of interior shared edges divided by the total number of perimeter edges. A higher ratio indicates a more compact, internally connected patch. Adding a well-positioned parcel to a patch raises this score. Methods Overview¶

Parcel data for Weld County were downloaded from the county's public GIS API and clipped to a the Pawnee National Grassland study boundary, yielding 3,476 parcels. Each parcel was classified as federal, state, or private based on the owner name field in the county dataset. Federal parcels were grouped into 166 contiguous patches using shared-edges (corner-touching does not count as contiguous). For each patch, an exposure value was calculated (fill in more here afer I do the inverse exposure math).

Candidate land swaps were identified by applying the following constraints. All parcel geometries were projected to an equal-area coordinate system (EPSG:5070) before any area or distance calculations were performed. Only federal patches with at least 2 parcels and a total area of 2,000 acres or more were considered as receive candidates, yielding 19 eligible patches. An acquire candidate is a non-federal parcel that shares a full edge (at least 1 meter of shared boundary) with a parcel in one of those 19 patches. A release candidate is a federal parcel on the outer boundary of a patch, whose removal would not disconnect the patch. This ensures that releasing a parcel does not fragment the federal block further. The acquire and release parcels in a proposal must also have centroids within 10 kilometers of each other, and their areas must be within 10% of one another. Proposals where the acquire parcel intersected an active or permitted oil and gas well from the Colorado Energy and Carbon Management Commission (ECMC) dataset were flagged. Remaining proposals were ranked by the net decrease in patch exposure produced by the swap.

All data are sourced from publicly available APIs; all code is available on GitHub and archived on Zenodo (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.19864164).

Figure 4. Example land swap proposals for the Western unit at Pawnee National Grassland, ranked by contiguity score gain. Green labels (A#) mark parcels proposed for federal acquisition from state ownership; red labels (R#) mark the federal parcels proposed for release in each exchange. Background shading reflects the current contiguity score of each federal land group (same scale as Figure 2). State parcels are shown in blue.

Limitations and Future Work¶

The current ranking is based solely on spatial contiguity gain and edge exposure decrease. Data to inform more ecologically minded swaps has been intentionally left out due to it's spatial sparseness across the landscape, and because land managers on the grassland will have a more accurate ecological understanding of the area. We encourage the users of this tool to supplement these swap recommendations with field surveys to ensure there is ecological value behind these land swap decisions.
